metadata.title: Metropolitan, Urban, and Rural Regions: How Regional Differences Affect Elementary School Students in Germany

ml_techniques.baseline_model: OLS baseline with state fixed effects

confounders_identified: Principal components derived from student survey (e.g., grades, skills, absenteeism/library usage/extracurricular reading, reading activities in class, perceived classroom management, perceived teacher support, sense of safety at school, private tutoring, participation in all-day activities, computer and internet use)

Principal components derived from parent survey (e.g., reference person, social background, reading habits of parents, number of books at home, parental education/occupation, economic and cultural capital, number of digital devices, preschool years/early reading preparation, parental support activities and parents’ interest in child’s friendships, parents’ satisfaction/contact with school)

Principal components derived from teacher survey (e.g., demographic/biographical info, teaching experience, phonics tables, classroom disturbances/constructivist beliefs/cognitive activation, spelling instruction, collaborative teaching, resources, differentiation in reading lessons, use of computers/internet in reading instruction)

Principal components derived from school principal survey (e.g., school climate/school spirit, school organization/performance orientation/classroom management, resources and equipment/free meals/homework supervision/computers, additional support services, measures for promoting reading, inclusion, immigration, information about students/teachers/school administration)
extraction.outcome_summary: Using representative PIRLS 2016 data for Germany (N=3,959 fourth-grade students), the study examined whether students’ regional context (metropolitan, urban, rural) was associated with academic track recommendations, enjoyment of school, and reading interest. Baseline OLS models with German federal state fixed effects showed U-shaped regional patterns for academic track recommendations and enjoyment of school, and positive (marginal) regional differences for reading interest. After multiple imputation, school-level bootstrapping, PCA-based dimension reduction, and post–double-selection LASSO with post-LASSO OLS, student-level information largely explained the regional differences, while adding school-level information tended to add noise. A post hoc policy-relevance categorization suggested that both policy-related and non-policy-related factors contributed to reducing regional disparities, with non-policy variables reducing academic track differences the most.
